lesson.title: Dots, Not Lines: Understanding Discrete Functions
lesson.summary: Discrete functions have domains made of separate, isolated values, so their graphs are scattered points rather than connected curves.
lesson.body:
A discrete function is a function whose domain consists of separate, isolated values rather than every real number along an interval. The word discrete comes from the same root as "distinct," and that is the right way to picture it: the allowed inputs are countable and separated by gaps, like the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, so the graph of a discrete function is a scattering of individual points, never a connected line or curve.

Discrete functions show up whenever the quantity you are counting only makes sense in whole units. You cannot sell 2.7 tickets, hire 4.5 employees, or buy negative one snack, so any function modeling those situations naturally restricts its domain to a specific set of separated numbers, usually the whole numbers or the integers, instead of all real numbers.

Consider a vending machine that charges 2 dollars per snack. The cost function is C(n) = 2n, where n represents the number of snacks purchased. Since you can only buy a whole number of snacks, the domain is the set {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...}. Evaluating the function at each allowed input gives C(0) = 0, C(1) = 2, C(2) = 4, and C(3) = 6. There is no meaningful value for C(1.5), because 1.5 snacks is not a real purchase, so that input is simply excluded from the domain rather than rounded or estimated.

Graphing C(n) = 2n over this restricted domain produces four separate dots at (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6), with visible empty space between them. It would be a mistake to connect those dots with a straight line, because doing so would suggest that every value between the dots, like n = 1.5, is also part of the function, when it is not. Even though the points are isolated, the relation still passes the vertical line test at every one of its allowed inputs: each n-value is paired with exactly one C-value, so it remains a genuine function, just one with a restricted, separated domain.

You can often tell a function is discrete just by reading the context of a word problem, even before a graph is drawn. Phrases like "the number of buses needed," "the number of students," or "the number of weeks" are strong signals that only whole-number inputs make sense, while phrases like "the number of hours" or "the distance traveled" usually allow any real number and point toward a continuous function instead. Learning to catch that signal in the wording of a problem is often more useful day to day than checking a finished graph, because it tells you how to set up the domain correctly before you ever plot a single point.

Recognizing discrete situations matters because it changes how you interpret a graph, a table, and even a rate of change. In later work you will meet functions built entirely from separate integer inputs, such as step functions that model bracketed costs, and the discrete versus continuous distinction you are learning here is exactly the lens that makes those graphs make sense instead of looking like broken lines.
